summary: Describes the TLS cipher suites built on single DES and IDEA, which were defined for TLS 1.0 and 1.1 and dropped from TLS 1.2. It records them for completeness and explains why they should no longer be used. This document is historic and was replaced by RFC 8996.

eli5.summary: Long ago, computers locked their messages with two old kinds of padlock. This note keeps a record of how those locks worked, but says they are too easy to pick now, so nobody should use them.

subtitle: Why two old encryption methods were removed from TLS 1.2 and should no longer be used.

tldr.problem: TLS versions 1.0 and 1.1 included cipher suites based on DES and IDEA, but both are now cryptographically weak or rarely implemented.
tldr.mechanism: This document specifies the DES and IDEA cipher suites for completeness and explains why they are no longer recommended: DES has only 56 bits of effective key strength and is vulnerable to brute-force attacks; IDEA, while stronger, saw almost no real-world use.
tldr.outcome: Both were removed from TLS 1.2 and later. RFC 8996 replaced this document.

today: RFC 5469 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 8996. Both DES and IDEA cipher suites have been removed from TLS 1.2 and later versions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
TLS versions 1.0 and 1.1 included cipher suites based on DES (Data Encryption Standard) and IDEA (International Data Encryption Algorithm). Both algorithms are no longer recommended for general use in TLS and have been removed from TLS 1.2.

This document specifies these cipher suites for completeness and discusses the reasons why their use is no longer recommended.
sections.eli5: TLS is how computers scramble messages. It used to support two old scrambling methods that are now considered bad choices.

sections.title: DES Cipher Suites
sections.content:
DES (Data Encryption Standard) is a block cipher approved as a US federal standard in 1976. Although it treats the key as 64 bits, DES provides only 56 bits of protection; 8 of the 64 bits are not used by the algorithm. DES uses a 64-bit block size.

Six cipher suites have been defined for using DES in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode in TLS: TLS_RSA_WITH_DES_CBC_SHA, TLS_DH_DSS_WITH_DES_CBC_SHA, TLS_DH_RSA_WITH_DES_CBC_SHA, TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_DES_CBC_SHA, TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_DES_CBC_SHA, and TLS_DH_anon_WITH_DES_CBC_SHA.

DES has an effective key strength of only 56 bits, known to be vulnerable to practical brute-force attacks for over 20 years. A 2006 paper describes a system that performs an exhaustive key search in less than nine days on average for under 10,000 USD. Single-DES cipher suites SHOULD NOT be implemented; if implemented, they SHOULD NOT be enabled by default, and existing implementations SHOULD consider removing them.
sections.eli5: DES is so weak that a modern computer can guess all possible keys in a few days. Nobody should use it anymore.

sections.title: IDEA Cipher Suite
sections.content:
IDEA (International Data Encryption Algorithm) is a block cipher designed by Xuejia Lai and James Massey. It uses a 128-bit key and operates on 64-bit blocks, making it much stronger than DES.

One cipher suite has been defined for using IDEA in CBC mode in TLS: TLS_RSA_WITH_IDEA_CBC_SHA.

While IDEA is cryptographically stronger than DES, the IDEA cipher suite for TLS has not seen widespread use. Most implementations either do not support it, do not enable it by default, or do not negotiate it when other algorithms (such as AES, 3DES, or RC4) are available. Rarely used code is a source of security and interoperability problems; the IDEA cipher suite SHOULD NOT be implemented by TLS libraries and SHOULD be removed from existing implementations.
sections.eli5: IDEA is actually a strong padlock, but almost nobody used it in TLS. Unused code causes problems, so it was removed too.
